plan.title: What Really Caused the 2008 Financial Crisis
plan.description: The story of the 2008 financial crisis, from the US housing boom and subprime mortgages to securitization, the fall of Lehman Brothers and the government response. Learn how risky loans turned into a global meltdown.

beats.narration: On September 15, 2008, one bank filed for bankruptcy and shook the whole world economy. How did a housing boom end like this?
Houses seemed like a sure bet. Prices climbed, lenders competed for business, and almost anyone could get a loan to buy a home.
Lenders began making subprime loans, meaning loans to borrowers with poor credit. Many came with low teaser interest rates that later jumped.
Normally, banks check a borrower's collateral, credit history and character. But now they could sell the loan right away, so checking mattered less.
So where did all those loans go? Wall Street bought them. Let's follow the money, step by step.

props.title: Where the loans went
props.subtitle: How risky mortgages became global investments

beats.narration: Homeowners paid their lenders. Lenders sold the loans to investment banks. The banks pooled thousands of them into mortgage-backed securities, sold to investors.
The share of subprime mortgages passed on to investors rose from 54 percent in 2001 to 75 percent in 2006.
Banks then re-sliced these securities into complex products called CDOs. Rating agencies gave many of them top AAA ratings, so they looked safe.

props.definition: A Collateralized Debt Obligation: mortgage-backed securities re-sliced into new investments, often rated AAA.

beats.narration: Banks also borrowed heavily to buy more of them, with leverage up to 40 to 1. A small loss could wipe them out.
Then house prices stopped rising. By early 2007, subprime defaults hit a four-year high, and the crisis began that summer.
Defaults rise, so securities lose value. Then fear spreads, and banks stop lending to each other, freezing credit across the whole system.
Losses hit insurers like AIG, which had sold protection against defaults. When the losses came, the debts came due, and they could not pay.
Countrywide, Bear Stearns, IndyMac, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac all failed or were rescued before Lehman.
Then came September 15, 2008. Lehman Brothers filed the largest financial bankruptcy in US history. About twenty-six thousand employees worldwide lost their jobs.

props.image_query: Wall Street New York stock exchange

beats.narration: The next day, the Federal Reserve lent up to 85 billion dollars to AIG. Lehman was allowed to fail, but AIG was not.
Treasury Secretary Hank Paulson then asked Congress for 700 billion dollars. That became the Troubled Asset Relief Program, or TARP.

props.label: TARP request to rescue the financial system

beats.narration: Treasury, the Federal Reserve and the FDIC launched emergency programs. They bought mortgage-backed securities, propped up banks and stabilized the financial sector.
Before the new president took office, the economy was shrinking more than 8 percent and losing 800,000 jobs a month.
No single villain caused it. Risky loans, securitization, leverage and fear combined. When lenders stopped caring who repaid, the whole system paid.

props.text: When lenders stop caring who repays, everyone ends up paying.

accuracy.reason: Most figures match the notes (54%→75%, $85B AIG, $700B, 26,000 jobs), but the opening stat is typo'd and several claims are loose, such as 'shrinking more than 8 percent' and Countrywide placed as failing before Lehman.

coverage.reason: It covers boom, subprime, securitization, CDOs, leverage, AIG, Lehman and TARP, but omits the Fed's actions beyond AIG, the housing bubble's causes and the lasting effects. Rating-agency conflicts get one line.

structure.reason: Clear chaptered arc from boom to collapse to response, with a chain-reaction build. The ending is slightly abrupt, and the 'before the new president took office' beat comes after TARP with no setup.

hook_ending.reason: The hook begins with Lehman and a question, which is decent but conventional. The ending line is a neat moral but the recap before it is a bare list.

tone.reason: Plain, accessible and neutral, suitable for a US general audience. It is a bit flat for a 'story'.

visuals.reason: Scene types vary well and match the narration. However, the first stat shows 'Sept 15, 200' (a typo), the checklist shows all unchecked boxes oddly, and the timeline repeats 2008 dates.

originality.reason: The 'three C's' dropped and the 40:1 leverage are specific, but the telling is mostly textbook with little vivid detail or human story.

instructions.reason: It includes all the requested elements and runs at about the target length. Storytelling is thinner than requested.

language.reason: Fluent and grammatical with short sentences. The fragment 'Lehman was allowed to fail, but AIG was not' is fine; there is some choppy repetition.

defects.issue: The on-screen date is truncated and wrong.

defects.quote: the economy was shrinking more than 8 percent
defects.issue: The source says the economy was shrinking at a rate of more than 8 percent, an annualized figure. The script drops that nuance and places the line after TARP without context.

defects.issue: Bear Stearns, Fannie and Freddie are glossed as 'failed or rescued', with no detail. Bear's JPMorgan-backed sale is a key moment that is skipped.

defects.quote: Treasury, the Federal Reserve and the FDIC launched emergency programs.
defects.issue: The response is vague, with no mention of rate cuts, bank capital injections, or lasting effects such as the Great Recession or Dodd-Frank.

defects.quote: Houses seemed like a sure bet.
defects.issue: The housing boom's causes (low rates, easy credit, speculation) are not explained.
A checklist with every box unchecked conveys 'ignored checks' only ambiguously.
